summary.brief: Chef Shane Lyons prepares, fries, and plates crispy buttermilk onion rings.
summary.detailed: The video opens with Shane Lyons cutting a large Spanish onion into thick, one‑inch rings and soaking them in a seasoned buttermilk mixture for a day. He makes a dry dredge from equal parts all‑purpose flour and tapioca starch, then prepares a wet batter that combines flour, beer, vodka, and buttermilk. Each ring is rolled in the flour, dipped in the batter with chopsticks, and gently lowered into hot canola oil heated to about 350 °F, frying for roughly three minutes until golden. The first batch is removed, drained, and frozen to remove excess moisture; after a brief defrost the rings are fried again, drained on paper towels over a stainless‑steel plate, seasoned with sea salt, topped with chopped scallions, an olive with black seasoning, and a small dish of preserved‑lime mayo, then presented on a plate.

action.detailed: Coat each onion ring in the flour‑tapioca dredge, dip it in the beer‑and‑vodka batter, lower it into hot oil to deep‑fry until golden, then drain, season with salt and garnish, and serve.

summary.brief: Chef Shane Lyons cuts a large Spanish onion, soaks the rings in seasoned buttermilk, coats them in a flour‑tapioca dredge and a beer‑vodka batter, deep‑fries them, then cools and briefly freezes them for extra crispness.
summary.detailed: The video opens with Shane Lyons selecting a large Spanish onion and slicing it into one‑inch‑thick rings while keeping the outer skin intact. He places the rings in a bowl of seasoned buttermilk with salt, pepper and a splash of additional buttermilk, letting them sit for about a day so the onion softens slightly. He then prepares a dry dredge of equal parts all‑purpose flour and tapioca flour and a wet batter that combines the same flours with beer, vodka and enough liquid to coat the rings. Using chopsticks to avoid getting batter on his hands, he first shakes each ring in the flour‑tapioca mixture, then dips it into the beer‑vodka batter, tapping off excess. He transfers the coated rings with tongs into hot canola oil heated to roughly 350 °F and fries them for about three minutes until golden brown. After frying, he removes the rings, lets them cool completely, and notes that briefly freezing them after the first cook helps the starches set, producing an even crisper texture for a later fry.

action.detailed: Coat the onion rings in a flour‑tapioca dredge, dip them in a beer‑vodka batter, and carefully drop them into hot oil to fry until golden, then cool and briefly freeze them for added crispness.
